messages.subject: binominal regression: se=T covers full data range
messages.subject_clean: binominal regression: se=T covers full data range
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have some dose/response data for which I want to plot a binominal regression with errors. When setting se=T in the geom_smooth function, the error covers the whole data range:

So, here's my data and the ggplot code:

df <- data.frame(x = c(83.3, 41.7, 20.8, 10.4, 5.2, 2.6, 1.3),
                 y = c(15, 15, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                 total = c(15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15))

ggplot(data = df,
       aes(x = x, y = y/total)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit")), aes(weight=total),  se=T, fullrange=F)

I'm
quite new to this and I can't figure out what the problem is. It works fine for my other data sets. The only difference is that for my other data the points don;t lie perfectly on the fitted line as they do in this plot. So the R^2 in this example would be 1. Could this cause problems?

I would appreciate some help here.

Cheers,
Ingo

messages.subject: Re: binominal regression: se=T covers full data range
messages.subject_clean: binominal regression: se=T covers full data range
messages.body_plain:
I think there are two issues here: First, logistic regression is appropriate when the outcome can be one of two categories which get dummy-coded as 0 or 1. In your case, the outcome is a proportion that can take on any real value between 0 and 1. I think beta regression is the appropriate method for such data (see, for example, the vignette for the betareg package: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/betareg/vignettes/betareg.pdf).

Second, in cases where logistic regression is appropriate, a problem that can arise is called "perfect separation." This occurs when there is at least on independent variable that allows you to predict with 100% percent certainty whether the outcome is 0 or 1. In such cases, there is not a unique solution for the regression coefficients, and the standard error for the regression line essentially covers the full range between probabilities of 0 and 1. For example, if you run the code below you'll get a warnings about the fit not converging and that "fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred," meaning there was perfect separation. Also, in the summary, note the huge standard errors on the coefficients.

df <- data.frame(x = c(83.3, 41.7, 20.8, 10.4, 5.2, 2.6, 1.3),
                 y = c(15, 15, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                 total = c(15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15, 15))

df$yt = df$y/df$total

m = glm(yt ~ x, weights=total, data=df, family=binomial)
summary(m)

The examples below use data appropriate for logistic regression and demonstrate cases where there is perfect separation and where there is overlap between the two possible outcomes:

# Perfect separation
set.seed(2)
df2 = data.frame(
  x = c(runif(20,0,9), runif(20,11,20)),
  y = rep(0:1, each=20)
)

ggplot(data = df2,
       aes(x,y)) +

  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",

              method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit")))

# Outcomes overlap
set.seed(2)
df3 = data.frame(
  x = c(runif(20,0,12), runif(20,8,20)),
  y = rep(0:1, each=20)
)

ggplot(data = df3,
       aes(x,y)) +

  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",

              method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit")))

messages.subject: plot excluding varying missing columns for different ID
messages.subject_clean: plot excluding varying missing columns for different ID
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I have a data set with hierarchical structure, that is, measure times nested within IDs. For some ID, some columns are entirely missing, whereas other columns are entirely missing for other ID. I am trying to figure out a code that could plot this situation for all ID, as the data from new ID are keep coming in. Specifically, I would like to get a plot that include all the columns that are not entirely missing. In other words, I don't need the column that is entirely missing, I need the columns with values (although they can have missing values, they are not entirely missing). Ideally, I hope I could get a geom_line() kind of plot that shows the time trend of all columns together in the same plot.

A replicable code for one group looks like below:

````
df=data.frame(
  id=c(rep(1,3),rep(2,3),rep(3,3),rep(4,3)),
  t=c(rep(c(0,1,2),4)),
  a1=c(rep(NA,3),rep(c(1.3,NA,1.6),3)),
  a2=c(rnorm(3),rep(NA,3),rep(c(1.5,NA,1.2),2)),
  a3=c(rep(c(2.5,NA,3.2),2),rep(NA,3),rnorm(3)),
  a4=rnorm(12)
)
df1=df[df$id==1,]
ggplot(df1)+
  geom_line(data=df1[!is.na <http://is.na>(df1$a1),],aes(y=a1,x=t,color='c1'))+geom_point(aes(y=a1,x=t,color='c1'))+
  geom_line(data=df1[!is.na <http://is.na>(df1$a2),],aes(y=a2,x=t,color='c2'))+geom_point(aes(y=a2,x=t,color='c2'))+
  geom_line(data=df1[!is.na <http://is.na>(df1$a3),],aes(y=a3,x=t,color='c3'))+geom_point(aes(y=a3,x=t,color='c3'))+
  geom_line(data=df1[!is.na <http://is.na>(df1$a4),],aes(y=a4,x=t,color='c4'))+geom_point(aes(y=a4,x=t,color='c4'))+
  scale_color_manual(values=c('c1'='red','c2'='yellow','c3'='blue','c4'='green'),labels=c('anx1','anx2','anx3','anx4'))+
  labs(x='time',y='value',title='trend')
````

The error:

````
Aesthetics must be either length 1 or the same as the data (1): x and y Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
````

I have intentionally made the data like this.The thing is, the error only shows when ID ==1, 2, 3, but not for ID==4, as the ID==4 dose not have a column that is entirely missing.

Thank you very much.

Best regards,

YA

messages.subject: Re: plot excluding varying missing columns for different ID
messages.subject_clean: plot excluding varying missing columns for different ID
messages.body_plain:
Hi YA,

You seem to be aware of the problem, so really you
want to avoid a call that doesn't have any plottable
observations. You could do this by replicating your
commands and dropping the relevant geom_line call
for each id level. Or you could use facet_wrap to
produce id-separated graphs, which seems much more
straightforward.

I hope this will be helpful:

```
library(tidyverse)
#
# df is the name of a function, so is best avoided as an object name
DF=data.frame(

   id=c(rep(1,3),rep(2,3),rep(3,3),rep(4,3)),
   t=c(rep(c(0,1,2),4)),
   a1=c(rep(NA,3),rep(c(1.3,NA,1.6),3)),
   a2=c(rnorm(3),rep(NA,3),rep(c(1.5,NA,1.2),2)),
   a3=c(rep(c(2.5,NA,3.2),2),rep(NA,3),rnorm(3)),
   a4=rnorm(12)
)

#
# Let's make the data long format to avoid all those calls
# to geom_line and use facet_wrap
DFl <- pivot_longer(DF, cols = paste0('a', 1:4))
#
# This should get you started...
gg1 <- ggplot(DFl) +
     geom_line(aes(x = t, y = value, colour = name)) +
     geom_point(aes(x = t, y = value, colour = name)) +
     facet_wrap(~ id, ncol = 2) +
     scale_color_manual(values = c('a1' = 'red', 'a2' = 'yellow', 'a3' =
'blue', 'a4' = 'green'),
                        labels = c('anx1', 'anx2', 'anx3', 'anx4'))+

     labs(x = 'time', y = 'value', title = 'trend')

# or maybe...
gg2 <- DFl %>% filter(!is.na <http://is.na>(value)) %>% ggplot(.) +
     geom_line(aes(x = t, y = value, colour = name)) +
     geom_point(aes(x = t, y = value, colour = name)) +
     facet_wrap(~ id, ncol = 2) +
     scale_color_manual(values = c('a1' = 'red', 'a2' = 'yellow', 'a3' =
'blue', 'a4' = 'green'),
                        labels = c('anx1', 'anx2', 'anx3', 'anx4'))+

     labs(x = 'time', y = 'value', title = 'trend')
```

Then print gg1 or gg2 to see them.

I used geom_point as well as geom_line to show where there
are actual data values. The second version should put a line
where there are two observed data points.

Regards,
Ron.
